stimulus: If the baker adds vanilla, the cake will be sweet. The baker added vanilla to the batter today.
choice_a: The cake is a chocolate cake.
choice_b: The cake will not be sweet.
choice_c: The baker forgot the sugar.
choice_d: The cake will be sweet.
explanation: Modus ponens application of the conditional statement.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Flavor is out of scope.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Contradicts the conditional.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Sugar is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_d: Correct. Direct result of the condition being met.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Burning is not mentioned.

stimulus: All employees at the firm wear suits. Jessica is an employee at the firm.
choice_a: Jessica wears dresses.
choice_b: Jessica wears a suit.
choice_c: Jessica is the boss.
choice_d: Suits are expensive.
explanation: Jessica is part of a group where everyone shares a characteristic.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Contradicts the premise.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Valid categorical logic.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Role is not specified.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Cost is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Preference is irrelevant.

stimulus: Only members of the committee can vote on the budget. Mark is voting on the budget.
choice_a: Mark is not on the committee.
choice_b: Mark wrote the budget.
choice_c: The budget will pass.
choice_d: Mark is a member of the committee.
explanation: Voting requires committee membership; since Mark is voting, he must be a member.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Contradicts the premise.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Authorship is out of scope.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. The outcome is unknown.
wrong_answer_d: Correct. Affirms the necessary condition.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Leadership role is not implied.

stimulus: Every time the alarm rings, the dog hides under the bed. The dog is not hiding under the bed.
choice_a: The alarm is ringing loudly.
choice_b: The alarm is broken.
choice_c: The alarm is not ringing.
choice_d: The dog is deaf.
explanation: Modus tollens; the absence of the necessary condition implies the absence of the sufficient condition.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Contradicts the logic.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Mechanical status is out of scope.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Valid contrapositive.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Hearing ability is out of scope.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Physical space is not discussed.

stimulus: To graduate with honors, a student must maintain a 3.8 GPA. Alice graduated with honors.
choice_a: Alice had a 4.0 GPA.
choice_b: Alice failed a class.
choice_c: Alice maintained at least a 3.8 GPA.
choice_d: Alice was the valedictorian.
explanation: Graduating with honors guarantees the GPA requirement was met.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. While possible, only a 3.8 is strictly required.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Unlikely if she maintained a 3.8, but not strictly impossible.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Fulfills the necessary condition.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Valedictorian status is not discussed.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Academic dishonesty is out of scope.

stimulus: No birds have scales. The pet in the cage has scales.
choice_a: The pet is a bird.
choice_b: The pet is a parrot.
choice_c: The pet is a fish.
choice_d: The pet is not a bird.
explanation: Because having scales excludes being a bird, the pet cannot be a bird.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Contradicts the premise.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. A parrot is a bird.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. It could be a reptile; cannot be proven it is a fish.
wrong_answer_d: Correct. Valid deductive inference.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Could be a fish or other scaled animal.

stimulus: If the wind speed exceeds 40 mph, the bridge will be closed to traffic. The wind speed is currently 55 mph.
choice_a: The bridge will be closed to traffic.
choice_b: The bridge is shaking.
choice_c: Traffic will be re-routed.
choice_d: The wind will die down soon.
choice_e: The bridge is made of steel.
explanation: The sufficient condition (wind > 40) is met, triggering the necessary result.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Direct application of the rule.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Physical movement is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Re-routing is a likely but unstated consequence.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Future weather is unknown.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Material is irrelevant.

stimulus: All novels in the library are fiction. This blue book is a novel in the library.
choice_a: The blue book is a biography.
choice_b: The blue book is non-fiction.
choice_c: The blue book is fiction.
choice_d: The blue book is a mystery.
explanation: The book belongs to a set defined as entirely fiction.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Biographies are non-fiction.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Contradicts the premise.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Direct categorical logic.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Genre subset is unknown.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Length is not discussed.

stimulus: Only registered patients can see the doctor today. Kevin is seeing the doctor today.
choice_a: Kevin is a registered patient.
choice_b: Kevin is a walk-in.
choice_c: Kevin is the doctor's friend.
choice_d: Kevin has an emergency.
explanation: Seeing the doctor guarantees Kevin meets the necessary condition of registration.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Valid application of the necessary condition.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Contradicts the requirement.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Friendship doesn't bypass the stated rule.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Medical status is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. ID status is not mentioned.

stimulus: Any product with a red sticker is discounted by 50%. This toaster has a red sticker.
choice_a: The toaster is full price.
choice_b: The toaster is broken.
choice_c: The toaster is discounted by 50%.
choice_d: The toaster is a popular item.
explanation: The toaster has the attribute that triggers the conditional rule.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Contradicts the rule.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Condition is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Modus ponens.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Popularity is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Color of the toaster is irrelevant.

stimulus: The mayor claims that painting crosswalks with bright yellow stripes will stop pedestrians from jaywalking, because the bright color will draw their attention to the designated crossing areas.
choice_a: Yellow paint fades quickly.
choice_b: Most jaywalking occurs because designated crosswalks are spaced too far apart, making them inconvenient.
choice_c: Drivers can see yellow stripes easily.
choice_d: Pedestrians often look at their phones.
choice_e: The city has a limited budget.
explanation: If convenience is the root cause of jaywalking, drawing attention to inconvenient spots won't change the behavior.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Fading is a maintenance issue, not a flaw in the initial behavioral logic.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Provides an alternative cause for the behavior the policy is trying to fix.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. This strengthens safety but doesn't address pedestrian behavior.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Phones distract, but doesn't strictly weaken the color-attention claim like B does.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Budget is irrelevant to efficacy.

stimulus: Taking a nap in the afternoon boosts productivity. We know this because workers who take 20-minute naps at 2 PM finish their daily tasks faster than those who don't.
choice_a: Naps can cause grogginess.
choice_b: Workers who take naps are also the ones allowed to leave work immediately upon finishing their tasks, incentivizing speed.
choice_c: Coffee also boosts productivity.
choice_d: Most offices do not have nap rooms.
explanation: Provides a massive confounding variable (incentive to leave) that explains the speed better than the nap itself.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. General fact that doesn't explain the specific study's results.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Introduces a strong alternative cause for finishing fast.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Alternative stimulants are out of scope.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Feasibility doesn't attack the causal claim.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Department variance doesn't apply if we assume a randomized or normalized study, but B is a direct attack.

stimulus: Because the new security guard started on Monday and theft dropped to zero on Tuesday, the new guard single-handedly eliminated theft in the store.
choice_a: The new guard is paid a high salary.
choice_b: The store also installed a highly visible, state-of-the-art camera system on Monday night.
choice_c: The new guard has no prior experience.
choice_d: Theft is a common problem in retail.
explanation: The camera system provides a highly likely alternative cause for the sudden drop in theft.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Salary doesn't affect the causal claim.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Offers a strong alternative explanation.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Lack of experience would weaken his capability, but the camera is a better direct attack on the causality.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. General industry fact.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Merchandise type is irrelevant.

stimulus: Switching to a plant-based diet cures acne. Many teenagers who stopped eating dairy and meat saw their skin clear up within months.
choice_a: Plant-based diets are expensive.
choice_b: Teenagers frequently outgrow acne naturally due to stabilizing hormones over a few months.
choice_c: Dairy is a known inflammatory agent.
choice_d: Some adults also suffer from acne.
explanation: Provides a natural, biological alternative cause for the clearing of skin during the teenage years.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Cost is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Introduces age and natural development as a confounding variable.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. This would actually strengthen the argument.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Adult acne is out of scope.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Nutritional value of meat doesn't address the acne claim.

stimulus: Using software tool X increases coding speed. Team A used tool X and finished their project in half the usual time.
choice_a: Team B used tool Y.
choice_b: Team A was assigned a project that was significantly less complex than usual.
choice_c: Tool X is open-source.
choice_d: Coding requires intense focus.
choice_e: Team A has many senior developers.
explanation: If the project was inherently easier, it explains the speed without attributing it to the tool.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Team B's tools are irrelevant.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Provides a strong alternative cause (lower difficulty).
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Cost/license is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. General fact about coding.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Seniority helps, but if it's the *same* team A as usual, the complexity change (B) is the variable that explains the difference.

stimulus: The new highway bypass will reduce noise pollution in the town center by diverting heavy truck traffic away from residential areas.
choice_a: The bypass is six lanes wide.
choice_b: Current noise pollution in the town center is almost exclusively generated by the heavy trucks that will now be required to use the bypass.
choice_c: The town center has many historic buildings.
choice_d: Residents have complained about noise for years.
choice_e: Electric trucks are becoming more common.
explanation: Confirms that the specific thing being diverted is the actual cause of the problem being solved.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Width is irrelevant to the town center's noise.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Links the solution directly to the root cause.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Historic status is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Complaints confirm the problem, not the solution's efficacy.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Electric trucks would reduce noise without the bypass, slightly weakening the *need* for it.

stimulus: Chewing mint gum improves test performance. Students who chewed mint gum during their final exams scored higher on average than those who didn't.
choice_a: Mint is a popular flavor.
choice_b: In a controlled lab setting, the scent and taste of mint were proven to stimulate the cognitive centers of the brain responsible for recall.
choice_c: Exams are highly stressful.
choice_d: Some students swallowed the gum.
choice_e: The students who chewed gum bought it themselves.
explanation: Provides a biological mechanism that explains exactly how the cause leads to the observed effect.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Popularity is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Adds scientific verification of the mechanism.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Stress is a general condition.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Irrelevant behavior.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Source of the gum is irrelevant.

stimulus: Because the factory installed a new ventilation system and employee sick days decreased, the new system improved employee health.
choice_a: The factory produces harsh chemical fumes.
choice_b: Other similar factories that did not install the system saw a simultaneous increase in employee sick days due to a regional flu outbreak.
choice_c: The ventilation system is energy efficient.
choice_d: Sick days are paid.
explanation: Shows that a control group (without the system) suffered, while the factory with it did not, strengthening the causal link.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Establishing the presence of fumes helps, but B provides comparative data.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Uses a control group to rule out a coincidental drop in sickness.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Efficiency is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Compensation is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Uniforms are irrelevant.

stimulus: Eating ginger reduces nausea. Pregnant women who consumed ginger root reported feeling much less morning sickness.
choice_a: Ginger is a root vegetable.
choice_b: Double-blind clinical trials confirmed that the active compounds in ginger block the exact neural receptors that trigger the nausea reflex.
choice_c: Morning sickness is common in the first trimester.
choice_d: Ginger can be consumed as tea.
choice_e: Many women dislike the taste of ginger.
explanation: Provides clinical proof of the exact biological mechanism linking ginger to the reduction of nausea.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Botanical classification is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Confirms the mechanism of action.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. General medical fact.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Method of consumption is secondary to efficacy.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Taste is irrelevant.

stimulus: The drop in local bird populations is caused by outdoor house cats hunting them.
choice_a: Cats are popular pets.
choice_b: When a strict indoor-only ordinance for cats was enforced for one year, the local bird population immediately recovered to historical levels.
choice_c: Birds eat insects.
choice_d: There are many stray dogs in the area.
explanation: Demonstrates that removing the suspected cause completely reverses the effect, strongly implying causation.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Popularity doesn't prove the hunting claim.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Validates the claim via a removal test.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Dietary habits of birds are out of scope.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Stray dogs offer a competing cause, which would weaken the claim.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Cost of food is irrelevant.

stimulus: Every piece of furniture in this room is incredibly heavy. Therefore, if we tie them all together, the resulting structure will be light and easy to carry.
choice_a: Assumes furniture can be tied together.
choice_b: Draws a conclusion about a whole that is the exact opposite of the properties of its parts.
choice_c: Attacks the furniture designer.
choice_d: Confuses weight with volume.
explanation: This is an inverted fallacy of composition; assuming heavy parts somehow make a light whole.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Tying them is a premise constraint, not the logical flaw.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Identifies the absurd part-to-whole deduction.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. No attack is present.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Volume is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Room size is irrelevant.

stimulus: Since this puzzle is made of 1,000 tiny, simple pieces, the completed puzzle must be a tiny, simple image.
choice_a: Assumes puzzles are for children.
choice_b: Attacks the puzzle maker.
choice_c: Confuses the properties of individual components with the property of the assembled unit.
choice_d: Assumes the puzzle is colorful.
explanation: Classic fallacy of composition; tiny pieces make a large, complex whole.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Age demographics are out of scope.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. No attack is present.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Identifies the part-to-whole logical error.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Color is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. The premise and conclusion are not identical.

stimulus: No one has ever definitively proven that the Loch Ness Monster does not exist. Therefore, we must accept that it lives in the lake.
choice_a: Confuses a lack of disconfirming evidence with positive proof of a claim.
choice_b: Assumes monsters are dangerous.
choice_c: Attacks Scottish folklore.
choice_d: Relies on outdated sonar data.
choice_e: Assumes lakes are deep enough for monsters.
explanation: Argument from ignorance fallacy.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Identifies the appeal to ignorance.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Danger is not discussed.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Folklore is not attacked.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Data is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Depth is not the logical issue.

stimulus: My neighbor's teenager was playing loud music yesterday. Clearly, all teenagers are utterly disrespectful menaces to society.
choice_a: Assumes music is bad.
choice_b: Draws a sweeping, absolute conclusion about an entire demographic based on a single instance.
choice_c: Attacks the neighbor's parenting.
choice_d: Confuses cause and effect.
explanation: Hasty generalization based on a sample size of one.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. The issue is the generalization, not the music itself.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Identifies the hasty generalization flaw.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Parenting is not mentioned.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. No causal mix-up.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Society's values are presumed, but the flaw is the demographic leap.

stimulus: Either we completely ban all cars from the city center, or our air quality will forever be toxic.
choice_a: Presents a false dilemma by ignoring moderate solutions like emissions standards or hybrid zones.
choice_b: Assumes cars are useful.
choice_c: Attacks drivers.
choice_d: Confuses sufficient and necessary conditions.
explanation: False dichotomy fallacy.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Identifies the false dilemma.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. The speaker likely thinks the opposite.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Drivers are not directly attacked.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. No conditional logic error.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Toxicity being bad is a reasonable assumption, not the logical flaw.

stimulus: Senator Vance argues we need to fix the potholes on Main Street. But Vance was once caught speeding, so his infrastructure plan is clearly garbage.
choice_a: Assumes potholes are dangerous.
choice_b: Dismisses a policy argument solely by attacking the character of the person proposing it.
choice_c: Confuses speeding with reckless driving.
choice_d: Assumes speeders don't care about roads.
explanation: Ad hominem fallacy.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Danger is not the core logical error.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Accurately describes the ad hominem attack.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Driving records don't invalidate infrastructure arguments.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. This is an assumption, but not the name of the flaw.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. It's an attack, not just an emotional appeal.

stimulus: The latest fashion magazine says neon green is the best color for summer, and millions of teenagers agree, so it must be the objectively best color.
choice_a: Relies on popular opinion and a single authority to establish an objective truth about a subjective matter.
choice_b: Assumes neon green is bright.
choice_c: Attacks fashion designers.
choice_d: Confuses summer with winter.
explanation: Appeal to popularity/authority fallacy on a subjective topic.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Identifies the ad populum flaw.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Brightness is a fact, not a flaw.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. No attack is present.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Seasons are not confused.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Buying habits are out of scope.

stimulus: If we let employees work from home one day a week, they will soon demand to work from home every day, and eventually, the office will be abandoned entirely.
choice_a: Assumes working from home is productive.
choice_b: Engages in a slippery slope fallacy, assuming an unstoppable chain reaction without evidence.
choice_c: Confuses a home with an office.
choice_d: Attacks the employees' work ethic.
choice_e: Assumes the office lease is expensive.
explanation: Slippery slope fallacy predicting extreme consequences.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Productivity isn't the core issue.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Identifies the slippery slope.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Definitions are not the issue.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. While implied, the *structure* of the flaw is the chain reaction.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Lease cost is out of scope.

stimulus: The new coffee shop will definitely be successful because it is located right next to the train station.
choice_a: Coffee is a healthy drink.
choice_b: Commuters who use the train station actually buy coffee during their daily transit.
choice_c: The train station is open 24 hours a day.
choice_d: The coffee shop has free Wi-Fi.
choice_e: The coffee shop is a franchise.
explanation: The location only guarantees success if the people at that location actually want the product.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Health is irrelevant to sales.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Connects the location to actual consumer behavior necessary for success.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. 24-hour operation isn't necessary, just busy enough hours.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Wi-Fi is a perk, not the core necessary assumption.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Franchise status is irrelevant.

stimulus: Switching our delivery trucks from gas to electric will save the company $10,000 a month in fuel costs.
choice_a: Electric trucks are quieter than gas trucks.
choice_b: The cost of electricity to charge the trucks is not greater than the $10,000 saved on gasoline.
choice_c: Gas prices are incredibly high right now.
choice_d: The company has 50 delivery trucks.
explanation: If electricity costs $11,000, they lose money. The argument assumes the alternate cost is lower.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Noise is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Defends the math from a catastrophic loophole.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Current gas prices are factored into the $10k claim; they don't need to be 'incredibly high'.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Fleet size is factored into the $10k claim.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Aesthetics are irrelevant.

stimulus: Because the candidate raised the most money during the campaign, she is guaranteed to win the election.
choice_a: Raising the most money is the only factor that voters consider when casting their ballots.
choice_b: The candidate is very charismatic.
choice_c: The opposing candidates raised very little money.
choice_d: Elections are held on Tuesdays.
choice_e: The candidate spent the money on television ads.
explanation: The argument takes one variable (money) and makes it the sole determinant of a complex outcome.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Identifies the extreme assumption required to guarantee a win.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Charisma might help, but isn't strictly assumed by the money logic.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. The relative amount is all that matters, not the absolute amount.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Day of the week is irrelevant.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Spending method is secondary to the assumption that money equals victory.

stimulus: Many people believe that stretching before a run prevents injuries. However, recent sports medicine studies show that cold stretching can actually cause micro-tears in the muscle. Therefore, runners should stick to dynamic warm-ups instead of static stretching.
choice_a: Stretching before a run prevents injuries.
choice_b: Cold stretching causes micro-tears.
choice_c: Runners should stick to dynamic warm-ups instead of static stretching.
choice_d: Running is a dangerous sport.
choice_e: Sports medicine is a new field.
explanation: The passage identifies a misconception, provides medical evidence, and concludes with a recommendation.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. This is the misconception.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. This is the premise/evidence.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Captures the author's prescriptive conclusion.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Not stated in the text.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Out of scope.

stimulus: While single-use plastics offer unparalleled convenience, they persist in the environment for centuries, choking marine life. Ultimately, governments must ban single-use plastics to preserve ocean ecosystems.
choice_a: Single-use plastics are convenient.
choice_b: Plastics persist in the environment for centuries.
choice_c: Governments must ban single-use plastics to preserve ocean ecosystems.
choice_d: Marine life is highly adaptable.
explanation: The text presents the conflict between convenience and ecology, ending with a policy demand.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Premise.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Premise.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Identifies the final conclusion and call to action.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. The text implies they are dying ('choking').
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. The text argues for a ban, not recycling.

stimulus: Open-concept offices were designed to foster collaboration. However, the constant noise and lack of privacy lead to massive decreases in deep-focus work. Businesses need to return to offering private offices to maximize employee output.
choice_a: Open-concept offices foster collaboration.
choice_b: Constant noise decreases deep-focus work.
choice_c: Businesses need to return to private offices to maximize output.
choice_d: Private offices are expensive to build.
explanation: The author outlines the failure of a design trend and concludes with a structural recommendation.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. This was the intended goal, not the author's point.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. Premise supporting the conclusion.
wrong_answer_c: Correct. Summarizes the author's proposed solution.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Cost is not discussed.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Music is out of scope.

stimulus: A popular streaming service dramatically increased its monthly subscription fee. Unexpectedly, the service saw a massive surge in new subscribers the following month.
choice_a: The streaming service added a highly anticipated, exclusive new season of the world's most popular television show on the same day the price increased.
choice_b: The streaming service changed its logo.
choice_c: Other streaming services lowered their prices.
choice_d: The economy entered a recession.
choice_e: The CEO of the streaming service resigned.
explanation: Explains how the negative impact of a price hike was overwhelmed by an even stronger positive incentive.
wrong_answer_a: Correct. Resolves the paradox by introducing an overriding motivation to subscribe.
wrong_answer_b: Incorrect. A logo change doesn't drive massive subscriptions.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. This would deepen the paradox; they should have lost subscribers to competitors.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. A recession usually reduces discretionary spending, deepening the paradox.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. CEO changes don't usually drive immediate subscription surges.

stimulus: Every time the city increases the police budget, crime rates go up the following year. Therefore, increasing the police budget actively causes more crime.
choice_a: Assumes police are well-trained.
choice_b: Fails to consider that an anticipated rise in crime might cause the city to preemptively increase the police budget.
choice_c: Attacks the police department.
choice_d: Confuses crime with minor infractions.
explanation: The argument confuses the direction of causation, missing that the effect (crime) might be anticipated, triggering the cause (budget).
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Training is out of scope.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Identifies the reverse causation flaw.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. No attack is present.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Categorization is not the issue.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Budget limits are not the logical error.

stimulus: We tested the new allergy pill on 10 healthy college athletes, and none reported feeling drowsy. Therefore, the pill will not cause drowsiness in the elderly.
choice_a: Assumes allergies are common.
choice_b: Draws a conclusion about a vulnerable population based on a sample of a highly resilient, non-representative population.
choice_c: Confuses drowsiness with fatigue.
choice_d: Assumes the pill is expensive.
explanation: Testing athletes to prove safety for the elderly is a severe unrepresentative sample flaw.
wrong_answer_a: Incorrect. Prevalence of allergies is out of scope.
wrong_answer_b: Correct. Accurately identifies the biased sampling flaw.
wrong_answer_c: Incorrect. Terminology is not the core issue.
wrong_answer_d: Incorrect. Cost is out of scope.
wrong_answer_e: Incorrect. Self-reporting is standard; the demographic is the flaw.

stimulus: To write a hit pop song, one must use a four-chord progression. Dave used a complex jazz progression, so his song will definitely not be a hit.
choice_a: Pop songs are always simple.
choice_b: Using a four-chord progression is the only way a song can become a hit.
choice_c: Dave is a bad musician.
choice_d: Jazz is unpopular.
